nodes.statement: In Section~ we give a proof of Lemma~ based on two technical lemmas, one about the concentration of a degree-related parameter (Lemma~), the other (Lemma~) facilitating the switching technique used in the proof of Lemma~. Lemma~ is proved in Section~, after giving some auxiliary results establishing the concentration of degrees and co-degrees in mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p) as well as in its conditional versions. In Section~, we present a proof of Lemma~, preceded by a purely deterministic result about alternating cycles in 2-edge-colored pseudorandom graphs. We defer some technical but straightforward results and their proofs (e.g., the proof of Claim ) to Section~. A flowchart of the results ultimately leading to the proof of Theorem~ is presented in Figure~.

In Section~\ref{sec_lemmaproof} we  give a proof of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw} based on two technical lemmas, one about the concentration of a degree-related parameter (Lemma~\ref{lem_thetas}), the other (Lemma~\ref{lem_ef}) facilitating the switching technique used in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem_Stanislaw}. Lemma~\ref{lem_thetas} is proved in Section~\ref{sec_degs_codegs}, after giving some auxiliary results establishing the concentration of degrees and co-degrees in $\mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p)$ as well as in its conditional versions.  In Section~\ref{sec_quasi}, we present a proof of Lemma~\ref{lem_ef}, preceded by a purely deterministic result about alternating cycles in 2-edge-colored pseudorandom graphs.
 We defer some technical but straightforward results and their proofs (e.g., the proof of Claim \ref{clm_sumofgammas}) to Section~\ref{sec_technical}.
 A flowchart of the results ultimately leading to the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm_embed} is presented in Figure~\ref{fig_flowchart}.

Let $B = B({\mathcal{R}}_{G,e}, {\mathcal{R}}_{G,\neg e})$ be the switching graph corresponding to the following forward switching: choose an alternating cycle $S$ of length at most $2D$ containing $e$ and switch the colors of edges within $S$. Note that the backward switching does precisely the same.
Note that by  the assumption, the minimum degree $\delta(B)$ is at least $1$.

Since  ${\mathcal{R}}_G={\mathcal{R}}_{G, e}\cup{\mathcal{R}}_{G, \neg e} \neq \emptyset$, one of the classes ${\mathcal{R}}_{G, e}$ and ${\mathcal{R}}_{G, \neg e}$ is non-empty and, in view of $\delta(B) \ge 1$, the other one is non-empty as well. For $\ell = 2, \dots, D$, the number of cycles of length $2\ell$ containing $e$ is, crudely, at most $n_1^{\ell - 1} n_2^{\ell - 1} = N^{\ell - 1}$, hence the maximum degree is
	\[
		\Delta(B)\le N + N^2 + \cdots + N^{D - 1} \le N^D - 1.
	\]
Thus, by~\eqref{eq_countingedges}, we obtain
 the claimed bounds.

nodes.statement: In this section we prove facts about the neighborhood structure of mathbb R(t), one of which will be enough to deduce Lemma~, while the other two will be used in the proof of Lemma~ in Section~. We start, in Subsection~, with a tail bound for the co-degrees in mathbb R = mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p) (Lemma~). In Subsection~ we analyze the process~(mathbb R(t))_t. First, we show that the vertex degrees in the process grow proportionally until almost the very end (Lemma~). Then, conditioning on mathbb R having concentrated co-degrees, we prove that the co-degrees in mathbb R(t) do not exceed their expectation too much (Lemma~). Finally, in Subsection~, we present a proof of Lemma~ based on Lemma~.

nodes.statement: Let xy be an edge with xin V_1, yin V_2. Without loss of generality, we assume that xy is blue. Then, by Lemma~, there exists at least one alternating walk from x to y of length at most 4lceil 16/rb rceil + 1 = 2D - 1 starting with a red edge. Consider a shortest such walk W. We claim W is a path. Indeed, assume that W is not a path and let w be the first repeated vertex on W. If we remove the whole segment of the walk between the first two occurrences of w, what remains is still an alternating walk from x to y starting with a red edge (since this segment has an even number of edges), contradicting the minimality of W. The path W is not just a single edge xy (since xy is blue) and therefore W and xy form an alternating cycle of length at most 2D.

nodes.statement: In view of Remark~, the error gamma in Theorem~ has optimal order of magnitude, whenever p le 1/4, provided that also p^2 mathbb I = Oleft( sqrtlog N / p hat n right) (that is, if either p = Oleft( left( (log N)/hat n right)^1/5right) or mathbb I = 0). From Remark~ it also follows that we cannot have gamma = o(1) for log N = Omega(phat n ). Theorem~ does not apply to the case log N ge phat n /(C^*)^2, but we think it would be interesting to find the largest p' for which one can a.a.s.\ embed mathbb G(n_1,n_2,p') into mathbb R(n_1,n_2,p) even in this case. The tightest embedding one can expect is the one permitted by the maximum degree. We conjecture that such an embedding is possible.

nodes.raw_latex:
\label{rem_large_p}
  For constant $p$, to obtain $\gamma = o(1)$ in Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}, we need to assume $\mathbb I = 0$, which requires a rather restricted ratio $n_1/n_2$. For example, one cannot afford $n_1 = n_2^{1+\delta}$ for any constant $\delta > 0$. This restriction comes from an enumeration result we use in the proof, namely, Theorem~\ref{thm_enum} (see condition~\ref{thm_enum_dense} therein). Should enumeration be proven with a relaxed condition, it would automatically improve our Theorem~\ref{thm_embed}.
